summary: 18 claims on lightning and workers, each checked against a fetched page or PDF. PDF text was read with a small local helper kept outside the repo. Global: the true toll is unknown. 3,806 deaths a year are documented in 30 nations, against an estimate of 24,000. US: NWS counts 21 deaths in 2025 and about 20 a year. About 18% of deaths are work-related (2006 to 2019). Construction has the highest worker death rate in national data (0.59 per million workers). Rules: wait 30 minutes after the last thunder, divide flash-to-bang seconds by 5, and stop lifts, scaffold, roofing and open-area work when lightning is within 10 miles (US Army Corps of Engineers manual). Other industries use 5 to 50 miles. Gulf: only single incidents (Saudi 2016, 2020, 2022), a south-west thunderstorm map, and the WMO record of 469 deaths at Dronka, Egypt, where lightning set fuel tanks on fire. No official Gulf count was found. Prediction: a NOAA-linked model gives a median 17.5 minutes of lead time. NOAA and OSHA still say no system can predict the first strike. Cost: the best reputable downtime numbers are modeled airport ramp closures (143 hours a year at Orlando under a strict 30/30 rule), not construction.

claims.topic: Global lightning deaths per year: estimate vs documented
claims.figure: 24,000 deaths and 240,000 injuries a year (estimate); 3,806 deaths a year documented in 30 nations
claims.measures: Status: stat (estimate and documented count). The 24,000 deaths figure was proposed in 2003 as six deaths per million people a year times four billion people in lightning-vulnerable places. The author calls both inputs subjective. The 3,806 figure is the recurring yearly total from published national studies for 30 countries (records span 1970 to 2022). The author says it is an undercount because many nations publish no lightning death totals. Abstract and section II on PDF p.1, Table I on PDF p.1-2. The same pair, 24 000 deaths and about 240 000 injuries a year, is printed in a peer-reviewed athletic trainers' position statement (https://www.nata.org/sites/default/files/2025-08/lightning_safety_for_athletics_and_recreation.pdf, PDF p.1). An older paper by the same author lists estimates of 6,000 to 24,000 a year and 4,101 deaths a year from 24 studies (https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/Ron%20Holle.%20Number%20of%20Documented%20Global%20Lightning%20Fatalities.pdf).
claims.region: Global (30 nations with published national studies)
claims.year: 2003 estimate; national records 1970 to 2022; paper c. 2023 (venue and year not printed, newest reference is 2023)
claims.source_title: A Year of Global Lightning Deaths and Injuries
claims.publisher: Conference paper hosted by the African Centres for Lightning and Electromagnetics Network (ACLENet)
claims.quote: proposed an annual global toll of 24,000 lightning deaths ... a recurring annual total of 3,806 lightning deaths per year
claims.use_in_story: Draw a wide band from 3,806 to 24,000 and label it nobody knows the true toll, which is the case for a measured data bank.

claims.topic: US lightning deaths: latest year and 10-year average
claims.figure: 21 deaths in 2025; about 20 deaths a year on average (10-year average, 2016 to 2025)
claims.measures: Status: stat. NWS yearly table (rows 2016 to 2026): 2025 = 3 female + 18 male = 21; 2024 = 14; 2023 = 14; 2022 = 20; 2021 = 11; 2020 = 17; 2019 = 22; 2018 = 21; 2017 = 16; 2016 = 40. The ten rows from 2016 to 2025 add up to 196 (my sum), which is 19.6 a year. The NWS lightning page says 'Lightning kills about 20 people in the United States each year, and hundreds more are severely injured.' (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning). The page heading on 2026-10-05 read 'National Weather Service Lightning Fatalities in 2026: 16', so 2026 is not a full year. Late reports raise counts: the archived NWS 2025 page says 20 (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-fatalities25) and the archived 2024 page says 13, while the current table shows 21 and 14. Triple-I repeats 21 for 2025 and 14 for 2024 and says 'On average, based on data from 2016 to 2025, 20 people die each year from lightning strikes'.
claims.source_title: National Weather Service Lightning Fatalities in 2026: 16 (yearly table 2016 to 2026)
claims.quote: Table row: 2025, Female 3, Male 18, Total 21. Text: Monthly averages are based on a 10-year average from 2016 to 2025.
claims.use_in_story: Tick a counter up to 21 and draw the 10-year average line at 20, to show the toll is small, steady and preventable.

claims.topic: Share of US lightning deaths that are work-related, 2006 to 2019
claims.figure: 77 of 418 deaths (18%) were work-related; inside that slice: farming/ranching 25%, construction 21%, roofing 17%
claims.measures: Status: stat. Study of all US lightning deaths 2006 to 2019 by the National Lightning Safety Council's safety specialist (PDF hosted by NWS, dated February 2020). Work-related means the victim was doing an activity that gave a significant part of their income. Other work shares: lawn care 9%, military 4%, other 25%. Construction plus roofing is 38% of work deaths (my sum of 21% and 17%). About 90% of work victims were male. Counts are on PDF p.5 (section 3.5: 418 deaths, 257 leisure, 68 daily routine, 77 work) and the work breakdown is on PDF p.8 (section 3.53). A newer 2006 to 2024 edition exists but could not be fetched (see gaps).
claims.source_title: A Detailed Analysis of Lightning Deaths in the United States from 2006 through 2019
claims.publisher: National Lightning Safety Council (PDF hosted by NOAA National Weather Service)
claims.quote: Work-related activities contributed to 18% of the total lightning fatalities.
claims.use_in_story: Draw a pie of the 418 deaths with an 18% work slice, then zoom into that slice and light up construction and roofing as 38% of it.

claims.topic: Latest NWS yearly tables: construction and roofing deaths 2023 to 2025
claims.figure: 3 construction or roofing deaths among 47 listed (2023: 14 rows, 2024: 13 rows, 2025: 20 rows); 7 rows show any work activity
claims.measures: Status: stat (my count of the NWS 'Activity' column, not an NWS-stated share). 2023 table: Construction (FL, age 24, location Rooftop), Roofing (NY, age 39, location Under tree), Working (AL, age 28, parking lot), On horse checking on cattle (NE, age 24). 2024 table: Roofing (FL, age 32, location Roof), Branding feeding cattle (CO, age 51). 2025 table: Working in forest (Dept.Nat.Res) (WI, age 48). The two cattle rows may be hobby or ranch work, so 5 to 7 work rows is the honest range. Row counts come from the archived yearly pages (2024 page: https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-fatalities24 shows 13; 2025 page: https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-fatalities25 shows 20). The current NWS summary table shows 14 and 21 for those years; I did not find the extra rows.
claims.source_title: National Weather Service Lightning Fatalities in 2023: 14 (with the 2024 and 2025 pages)
claims.quote: 2023 table: Rooftop, Construction; Under tree, Roofing. 2024 table: Roof, Roofing.
claims.use_in_story: Show three rows of dots, one per year, and flash the construction and roofing dots to say it still happens to site workers today.

claims.topic: Construction has the highest worker lightning death rate in US national data
claims.figure: Construction 0.59 deaths per million workers (agriculture, forestry, fishing 0.45; all work 0.12); 129 work-related deaths, 39 in construction
claims.measures: Status: stat. US national data from the NCHS death records and the Bureau of Labor Statistics fatal-injury census, 1995 to 2002. Industry table (PDF p.5, journal p.48): construction 39 deaths (30%), rate 0.59 (interval 0.42 to 0.81); agriculture, forestry, fishing 44 deaths (34%), rate 0.45 (0.34 to 0.62). The intervals overlap, so 'highest' is a point estimate. The abstract (PDF p.2) also says one of every four struck-by-lightning deaths in 1995 to 2002 was work-related, and 92 percent of work deaths came from May through September. Old data, but peer reviewed and national.
claims.source_title: Struck-by-Lightning Deaths in the United States (Journal of Environmental Health, May 2005; copy on the BLS site)
claims.publisher: Journal of Environmental Health (NEHA), republished by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics
claims.quote: A total of 129 work-related lightning deaths occurred during 1995-2002 (an average annual rate of 0.12 deaths per million workers).
claims.use_in_story: Show a bar chart of deaths per million workers by industry with the construction bar glowing, and say plainly the data is old and US only.

claims.topic: Jobs OSHA and NOAA list as higher lightning risk, and the OSHA storm bans
claims.figure: 13 listed job activities (my count of the bullets), including roofing, construction, heavy equipment and steel erection; OSHA bans scaffold, crane hoist and wall-top work in storms or high winds
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance and rule). Fact sheet FS-3863 dated 06/2021, issued by OSHA with NOAA. Full list (PDF p.1): Logging; Explosives handling or storage; Heavy equipment operation; Roofing; Construction (e.g., scaffolding); Building maintenance; Power utility field repair; Steel erection/telecommunications; Farming and field labor; Plumbing and pipe fitting; Lawn services/landscaping; Airport ground personnel operations; Pool and beach lifeguarding. PDF p.4 (bullet list): during storms or high winds OSHA prohibits work on or from scaffolds (29 CFR 1926.451(f)(12)), crane hoists (29 CFR 1926.1431(k)(8)) and work on top of walls (29 CFR 1926.854(c)). PDF p.1: lightning 'can strike outside the heaviest rainfall areas or even up to 10 miles from any rainfall.' PDF p.2: the written emergency plan should 'Indicate response times necessary for all workers to reach safe shelters.'
claims.source_title: Lightning Safety When Working Outdoors (OSHA and NOAA fact sheet FS-3863)
claims.publisher: US Department of Labor, OSHA, with NOAA
claims.quote: Worker activities at higher risk for lightning hazards include: Logging; Explosives handling or storage; Heavy equipment operation; Roofing; Construction (e.g., scaffolding)
claims.use_in_story: Show these job types as icons that turn red on a lightning alert, and link the three OSHA storm bans to the work-at-height and crane-lift permit types.

claims.topic: Deadliest lightning event on the WMO record is in Egypt and involved fuel storage
claims.measures: Status: stat (WMO-accepted record). A WMO panel accepted this as the 'highest mortality (indirect strike) associated with lightning'. A flash of lightning ignited three oil storage tanks, each holding about 5000 tons of aircraft or diesel fuel, and floodwaters swept the burning fuel into the village. The 469 comes from an Egyptian Ministry of Health and Population document ('hospitals ... had received 469 bodies'); an additional 63 flood deaths were reported separately. The same paper accepts 21 people killed by one flash in a hut in Zimbabwe (23 December 1975) as the highest direct-strike toll. Abstract on PDF p.1, Dronka section on PDF p.3 to 4 (journal p.489 to 490).
claims.source_title: WMO Assessment of Weather and Climate Mortality Extremes: Lightning, Tropical Cyclones, Tornadoes, and Hail
claims.publisher: Weather, Climate, and Society 9(3), 487-497 (American Meteorological Society), WMO Commission for Climatology panel; NOAA repository copy
claims.quote: 469 people killed in a lightning-caused oil tank fire in Dronka, Egypt, on 2 November 1994
claims.use_in_story: Use it as the regional wake-up call: lightning can ignite fuel stores, so tie lightning alerts to hot-work and fuel-handling permits.

claims.topic: Saudi Arabia: a lightning incident reported with a Civil Defense source
claims.figure: 2 dead and 2 injured by lightning, Al-Qunfudhah (Makkah province), November 2016
claims.measures: Status: stat (press report of one incident, not a count). The spokesman of Makkah Civil Defense is the named source in the article; the injured were taken to the nearest hospital. Two more press reports of single incidents: 5 August 2020, one person struck at a park in Najran, Najran civil defense directorate gave first aid (https://gulfnews.com/amp/world/gulf/saudi/pakistani-man-struck-by-lightning-in-saudi-arabia-1.72986708); 2 September 2022, one killed and one injured at Muhail in Asir, source given as the Sabq news portal (https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/saudi/lightning-strike-kills-27-year-old-man-injures-wife-in-saudi-arabia-1.90283931). All three are in the south-west provinces. No national yearly count was found.
claims.source_title: Two dead after being struck by lightning
claims.quote: Two residents died on Tuesday in Al-Qunfudah province after lightning struck them, with two others injured in the same incident.
claims.use_in_story: Pin the three incidents on a Saudi map in the south-west to show the risk is real here, then note that we found no yearly national count.

claims.topic: Saudi thunderstorm map: where lightning is most frequent
claims.figure: Thunder-days-per-year map built from 1985 to 2003 records; highest in the south-west (Abha, Taif, Al-Baha)
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed map, abstract read). Built from lightning-incidence records at the national weather service of the time (Presidency of Meteorology and Environment). Annual thunderstorms are most frequent over the south-western parts and decrease towards the west and east; the Red Sea west coast has the lowest count; a secondary maximum lies in the south-east to central part; no widespread trend over time; thunderstorm frequency does not follow rainfall. The abstract gives no thunder-day numbers. They are in the maps in the full paper, which was not read.
claims.source_title: Thunderstorm distribution and frequency in Saudi Arabia
claims.publisher: Journal of Geophysics and Engineering 2(3), 252 (Oxford Academic)
claims.quote: The southern region in general, and especially the cities of Abha, Taif and Al-Baha, has shown greater numbers of thunderstorm days all year round.
claims.use_in_story: Shade the south-west of a Saudi map as the lightning belt and place Connected Environment sites on it.

claims.figure: 30 minutes after the last thunder or lightning
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance). NWS 'Lightning Tips' page. NWS 'Overview: Lightning Safety' says 'Wait 30 minutes after the last lightning or thunder before going back outside.' (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-safety-overview). The OSHA and NOAA worker fact sheet says 'Remain in the shelter for at least 30 minutes after hearing the last sound of thunder' (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3863.pdf, PDF p.2). The athletic trainers' position statement says activities stay suspended until 30 minutes after the last strike or thunder, the clock restarts at each new flash within 5 nautical miles or thunder, and 'Waiting 30 minutes ... yields 90% to 95% confidence that no more lightning will occur' (https://www.nata.org/sites/default/files/2025-08/lightning_safety_for_athletics_and_recreation.pdf, PDF p.3 and p.9).
claims.quote: Stay in safe shelter at least 30 minutes after you hear the last sound of thunder.
claims.use_in_story: Run a 30-minute countdown ring that restarts on every new strike and turns green only for the all-clear.

claims.figure: Divide the seconds by five to get miles; 30 seconds or less means act now
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance). NWS 'JetStream' training page: 'Divide the number of seconds by five to get the distance the lightning is away from you' and 'Do not resume outdoor activities until 30 minutes after the last thunder clap.' The NWS thunder page (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder) gives 5 seconds = 1 mile, 15 seconds = 3 miles, and says thunder 'can be heard for a distance of only about 10 miles from the lightning strike'. A vendor paper warns the count has limits: thunder may not be heard in wind or rough terrain and can be matched to the wrong flash (https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.5).
claims.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service (JetStream training page)
claims.quote: If lightning is seen and the time delay to its subsequent thunder is 30 seconds or less
claims.use_in_story: Animate a flash, a counter and a circle that grows one mile every five seconds, to show why a sensor reading beats a human count.

claims.topic: Construction stop-work rule: lifts, scaffold, roofing and open-area work stop; 10 miles and 30 minutes (US Army Corps of Engineers manual)
claims.figure: 10 miles; resume 30 minutes after the last thunder or lightning
claims.measures: Status: stat (rule quoted second hand). The page prints paragraph (4) under 'Emergency Planning Section 01.E.01' of the US Army Corps of Engineers Safety and Health Requirements Manual EM 385-1-1. In the same paragraph, when lightning is observed all load handling equipment (cranes and lifts), drill rigs, work on elevated platforms or scaffolding, roofing, tree trimming, pole climbing and work in open areas must stop, and someone must judge how close the lightning is to the work. It also gives the divide-by-5 count. The page does not print an edition date, and the USACE host could not be reached from the fetch tool, so the primary text was not read. A vendor paper says the National Lightning Safety Institute advises construction workers to be aware when lightning is 20-40 miles from the site and to suspend work and evacuate when it is within 10 miles (https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.3). The same paper rates construction lightning risk 'High' and safety-tool adoption 'Low'.
claims.year: Edition not printed on the page
claims.source_title: 500 EM385-1-1 Construction Safety Hazard Awareness for Contractors, Sections 1-6 (quotes EM 385-1-1)
claims.publisher: OSHAcademy (quoting US Army Corps of Engineers EM 385-1-1)
claims.quote: If lightning is 10-miles away or less, work should stop until 30-minutes after the last audible thunder or visible flash of lightning.
claims.use_in_story: Draw a 10-mile ring around a site that flips lifts, drill rigs, scaffold, roofing and open-area work to Stop and starts the 30-minute clock.

claims.topic: Typical alert radii used by authorities and industries
claims.figure: 5 nautical miles (roughly 6 statute miles or 9.26 km) for sports; NCAA 8 miles; airports 10 and 5 miles; wind farms 50 and 30 miles; WMO stations 8 km and 8-16 km
claims.measures: Status: stat (guidance, mixed sources). Primary: the athletic trainers' position statement (J Athl Train 2013;48(2):258-270, PDF p.3, recommendations 15 and 17) says everyone must be fully inside a safe place when the edge of the lightning storm reaches 5 nautical miles, and activity stays suspended until 30 minutes after the last strike seen within 5 nautical miles. Sydney 2000 Olympics used three stages: yellow 60 minutes from the storm, orange 30 minutes, red when lightning is within 10 km (PDF p.9). Other documents: NCAA 8-mile radius with a 30-minute all-clear, and wind farms notify at 50 miles, stop work at 30 miles with a 15-minute all-clear (vendor paper, 2010, https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.3-4); Denver airport advisory at 10 miles, warning at 5 miles, secure after 15 minutes with none within 5 miles, and 5-mile and 3-mile limits recommended by airline trade bodies (ACRP Report 8, https://www.idc-online.com/technical_references/pdfs/electrical_engineering/acrp_rpt_008.pdf, PDF p.36-37); WMO reports a thunderstorm at an automated station for lightning within 8 kilometres and 'in the vicinity' at 8 to 16 km (WMO-No. 1198, https://amc.namem.gov.mn/wp-content/uploads/WMO/21.%201198_en.pdf?_t=1638837870, PDF p.15). The vendor paper's rule of thumb: start at 6 miles and add 1 mile for each 2 minutes of evacuation time.
claims.region: United States (sports, airports, wind farms), Australia (Sydney 2000), WMO (global)
claims.source_title: National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Lightning Safety for Athletics and Recreation
claims.publisher: Journal of Athletic Training (National Athletic Trainers' Association)
claims.quote: reaches 5 nautical miles (nmi; roughly 6 statute miles or 9.26 km
claims.use_in_story: Show nested rings for alert, warning and stop, and let each industry's ring size differ, so the platform needs a per-site setting.

claims.topic: Downtime and cost of a strict 30/30 lightning rule (airport ramps, modeled)
claims.figure: Orlando: 126 events and 143 hr in 2006; Chicago O'Hare: 68 ramp closures and 70.8 hours (approximately 1% of the time); 10 minutes shorter closures save approximately $2.8 million (Orlando) and $6.2 million (Chicago) a year
claims.measures: Status: stat (modeled, not measured). 2006 lightning-network data run through a strict 30/30 rule (stop when lightning is within 6 miles, restart 30 minutes after the last strike) to build 'synthetic' closure histories. The report says the results 'therefore do not represent actual reported lightning duration delays'. Savings use FAA 2007 economic values (for example $1,524 per aircraft-hour of delay, ramp labor $13.03 per hour, value of a human life $3.0 million, PDF p.13). Summary PDF p.12-13, Chicago PDF p.46, Orlando PDF p.50. It also says the AMS and NOAA have endorsed the '30-30 rule' (PDF p.24). Airport ramps, not construction. Official record of the report (title and year 2008 confirmed, text not extractable there): https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/14192/chapter/2.
claims.region: United States (Chicago O'Hare and Orlando airports)
claims.source_title: ACRP Report 8: Lightning-Warning Systems for Use by Airports
claims.publisher: Transportation Research Board, Airport Cooperative Research Program (sponsored by the FAA); copy hosted by idc-online.com
claims.quote: 68 ramp closures in 2006, with a total closure time of 70.8 hours, or approximately 1% of the time
claims.use_in_story: Count a stoppage clock up to 143 hours a year to show the price of a blunt rule, then show better lightning data shrinking it.

claims.figure: $1.65 billion paid, 61,986 claims, $26,616 average cost per claim (2025)
claims.measures: Status: stat. Triple-I table: 2025 value of claims $1,649.8 million, 61,986 claims, average $26,616; 2024 $1,035.3 million; 2020 peak $2,066.7 million. Homeowners property claims only. It is not a worker or construction cost, so use it as a scale marker only. The same page prints 'there were 21 direct lightning fatalities in 2025, compared to 14 in 2024.'
claims.quote: National claim increased 59.4 percent (from $1.04 billion) to $1.65 billion
claims.use_in_story: Use it as a property-loss scale marker, and say site equipment and downtime are not in this number.

claims.topic: NOAA-linked lightning nowcast: how many minutes of warning
claims.figure: Median lead time 17.5 min to the first lightning flash; 'frequently ... 20 min or more'; a quarter of hits 32.5 min or more; 0-60-min forecast window
claims.measures: Status: stat (published verification, satellite model). LightningCast by scientists at NOAA/NESDIS and the University of Wisconsin (CIMSS), trained on GOES satellite images. Test: GOES-16 CONUS scenes, the 5th to 9th of each month of 2020, points about every 80 km. With the lightning-onset criterion the median lead time to the first flash is 17.5 min at the 30% and 40% probability thresholds (12.5 min without the criterion), and a quarter of true-positive predictions measured 32.5 min or more (PDF p.13, journal p.1251). The output is a probability for the next 60 minutes, not a certainty. CIMSS blog, 31 January 2025: version 2 'will be operational at NOAA later in 2025' (https://cimss.ssec.wisc.edu/satellite-blog/archives/62924). WMO defines nowcasting as 'from the present to 6 hours ahead' (WMO-No. 1198, PDF p.11) and says lightning detection systems 'increase warning lead times for dangerous thunderstorms' without giving a minute figure (PDF p.19).
claims.region: United States (CONUS test); model also runs on GOES full disk
claims.source_title: ProbSevere LightningCast: A Deep-Learning Model for Satellite-Based Lightning Nowcasting
claims.publisher: Weather and Forecasting 37(7), 1239-1257 (American Meteorological Society); NOAA repository copy
claims.quote: LightningCast, which frequently provides 20 min or more of lead time to new lightning activity
claims.use_in_story: Show a probability bar rising ahead of the first strike with a bracket of about 17 to 20 minutes, which is the time a work plan has to pause lifts.

claims.topic: No system can predict the first lightning strike
claims.figure: None: no system can detect the first strike, detect all lightning, or predict strikes (NOAA and OSHA)
claims.measures: Status: stat (official caution). The fact sheet says commercial detection and notification services can send alerts when lightning develops or moves within a set range of a work site, but cannot predict the first strike, so workers must watch the sky and reach shelter before the first strike. NOAA recommends employers first rely on NOAA weather reports. Handheld detectors are described as less accurate than commercial networks. PDF p.3.
claims.source_title: Lightning Safety When Working Outdoors (OSHA and NOAA fact sheet FS-3863)
claims.publisher: US Department of Labor, OSHA, with NOAA
claims.quote: no systems can detect the "first strike," detect all lightning, or predict lightning strikes.
claims.use_in_story: Be honest on the slide: show lead time as a probability with a margin, and keep a human stop rule on top.

claims.topic: Farm work in one year of global lightning news reports (2021), and the Gulf gap
claims.figure: Farming named in 125 incidents, 185 deaths and 143 injuries; all reports: 505 incidents, 765 deaths, 560 injuries, 46 nations; no Gulf nation among them
claims.measures: Status: stat (media-based sample, biased). The author searched hourly Google Alerts for the English word 'Lightning' for calendar year 2021: 'A total of 505 incidents were found including 765 deaths and 560 injuries from 46 nations; half are from India.' The Indian subcontinent has 320 of the 505 incidents. Table IV (PDF p.3) lists no Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain; Israel and Turkey are listed under Europe. Absence in an English-news method is not proof of no incidents. Single-victim events are under-reported (only 42% of incidents involve one person, against 93% in the US). Caution: the paper also prints 'Farming accounts for 35% of the events', but 125 of 505 is 24.8% and 185 of 765 deaths is 24.2% (my arithmetic), so use the counts, not the 35%. Farm sentence is in section VII.
claims.region: Global (46 nations; half of reports from India)
claims.source_title: A Year of Global Lightning Deaths and Injuries
claims.publisher: Conference paper hosted by the African Centres for Lightning and Electromagnetics Network (ACLENet)
claims.quote: There are 125 incidents, 185 deaths, and 143 injuries included in the reports.
claims.use_in_story: Show a world map where farm and outdoor-labour incidents pop up, and leave the Gulf blank to show nobody is counting there yet.

gaps: No official Saudi or Gulf (GCC) lightning death or injury count was found. Only single incidents reported by press (Makkah 2016 and Najran 2020 cite civil defense, Asir 2022 cites a news portal) and a 2005 thunder-day map. A Saudi Civil Defense news item about two deaths from lightning at Al-Soudah in Asir (https://998.gov.sa/Ar/Accidents/Pages/news-2971430.aspx) did not render in the fetch tool, so its date and count are unverified. The shared WebSearch budget (200 of 200) ran out before Kuwait, UAE, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain and Saudi National Center for Meteorology statements could be searched in full, so such a statement may exist.

The Gulf is absent from the 2021 global news dataset (no Saudi, UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain entry in Table IV, PDF p.3 of https://aclenet.org/file_download/21dc2171-cc21-4b66-b02b-cd29c514ad93). That shows a data gap, not a safe region.

The Saudi Civil Defense public page 'The risk of lightning' (https://998.gov.sa/en/Page/riskoflightning/web//Marquee/, shown as last updated 2026-01-01) gave qualitative advice only: the full body text, printed by the fetch tool, has no number of miles, minutes or seconds, no thunder-count rule and no statistics. It is a machine-translated page, so it may differ from the Arabic original.

No global occupational share of lightning deaths exists in ILO, WHO or WMO material that I could reach. Proxies used: US work share 18% (2006 to 2019) and one in four (1995 to 2002); farming named in 185 of 765 deaths in 2021 English news; and an Eastern Turkiye autopsy study where 9 of 13 lightning deaths (69.2%) were shepherds (Eurasian J Med 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13324915/, 847 forensic autopsies 2019 to 2025). Not used as a claim because it is 13 cases.

The newer US analysis for 2006 to 2024 is cited by search summaries as 95 work-related deaths of 492 (19%), with farming/ranching 24%, roofing 21%, construction 17% of work deaths. I could not fetch it (lightningsafetycouncil.org returned a TLS error), so I used the 2006 to 2019 edition hosted by NWS. The order of roofing and construction differs between the two editions.

No reputable lightning downtime or cost figure for construction sites was found. Closest are the modeled airport numbers in S2-14 and a vendor blog (lightningprotection.com, 24 April 2013, https://www.lightningprotection.com/protecting-against-catastrophic-lightning-strikes/) saying a construction company at a Singapore refinery expansion lost 'nearly one full work day each week' and a Dominican Republic mine lost '40 hours per worker per month'. No study sits behind the vendor claims. A weather-delay cost of $7 to 8 billion a year for US construction showed up only in search summaries of secondary blogs and was not used. The MDPI weather-delay review (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/5/2861) returned 403.

Wind-industry number not used as a claim because it is a vendor report: 'Lightning damage costs the wind industry more than $100 million a year and accounts for 60% of blade losses' and '2.01 billion total lightning events detected in 2025' (Xweather Annual Lightning Report 2025, https://xweather.com/annual-lightning-report). Same page: 252 million US strikes in 2025, an eight-year high.

WMO: no WMO statement of global lightning deaths and no lightning-specific lead-time number was found. A WMO-attributed 'about 2,000 deaths a year' appeared only in a search summary, never on a fetched page, so it is not used. The WMO nowcasting page on wmo.int returned 404; the WMO-No. 1198 text was read from a copy hosted by a national meteorological agency.

A lightning-jump algorithm gives an average lead time of 21.15 minutes (standard deviation 14.68) for severe weather, with probability of detection 82% and false alarm rate 35% (NASA NTRS record 20110008658, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110008658). It measures severe-weather lead time, not lightning, so it is not a claim here.
The EM 385-1-1 primary text (US Army Corps of Engineers) could not be reached (DNS failure for usace.army.mil), so the 10-mile rule is cited from a training-site quote and rated medium.

India: the national crime records report for 2022 says lightning was 35.8 per cent of 8,060 accidental deaths from forces of nature (Down To Earth, 4 December 2023, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/governance/over-8-000-accidental-deaths-in-2022-due-to-forces-of-nature-35-due-to-lightning-ncrb-93177). That is about 2,886 deaths by my arithmetic. The primary PDF is over 10 MB and was not fetched.

Dated or blocked sources: the OSHA fact sheet still says 'about 50 people, on average, have been killed by lightning strikes every year' over 30 years, which NWS now puts near 20, so treat it as dated. Springer (2025 US lightning mortality paper 1979 to 2023), AMS (2016 review abstract) and ResearchGate pages returned 403 or a cookie redirect and were not read. Author and spokesperson names are left out on purpose; each claim is traceable by title, publisher and URL.
